fields.meta_title: Category Landing Page Examples and Builder | Emergent
fields.meta_description: A category landing page helps shoppers find the right product fast. See four working examples, then build yours from a prompt. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Category Landing Page Shoppers Can Filter
fields.hero_description: Get a category landing page with product filters and a catalog table you own, built from a single prompt.
fields.features_subheading: A category page answers one question for a shopper: which of these is mine? Emergent builds the parts that help them decide.
fields.feature_1:
A grid read from your product table

Emergent builds the grid from a product table in a database you own. Add a shoe to the table, and it shows up on the page with its price, its photo and a link to its page.
fields.feature_2:
Filters drawn from product attributes

Shoppers narrow the grid by the attributes stored in each row, such as width or cushion. Name the filters you want in the prompt, and the app shows how many products match each.
fields.feature_3:
Subcategory tiles with click counts

Each subcategory tile links to its own page, and the app records every click on it. The counts land in a table you can sort, so you can see which tile has earned its place.
fields.feature_4:
Prices and stock from your store

Connect your store platform through its API, and each product card shows the price and stock it reports. Slack or HubSpot connect the same way for an alert or a CRM record.
fields.feature_5:
New subcategories added by prompt

Ask for a change in plain English, such as "Add a Rain Shells tile after Jackets." Emergent updates the page, and the intro copy and the filters change the same way when you ask.
fields.feature_6:
Your code on your domain

Export the page to your GitHub repository on paid plans, or keep it hosted on Emergent under a custom domain, which uses credits. Either way, the products stay in a database you own.

fields.usecase_heading: Category Landing Page Examples by Goal
fields.tab_content_1:
Of 48 trail shoes, 6 pass both filters

Juniper Ridge Outfitters sells 48 trail running shoes, and its category page reads every one from the product table. A shopper picks Wide fit, then Max cushion, and the grid drops to the 6 shoes that match both filters. Each card still shows its price and the stock count from the table.
fields.tab_content_2:
Floor lamps took first place after 30 days

Over 30 days, 3,000 visitors clicked a subcategory tile on Halden Home's lighting page. Floor lamps drew 1,350 clicks, pendants 900, table lamps 480, and sconces 270. The team asked Emergent to move floor lamps into the first tile and put the other 3 tiles in click order.
fields.tab_content_3:
Who quotes the job depends on roof size

Commercial roofing jobs at Corbel Roofing start on a category page that lists its 3 services above a quote form. A request for a roof over 20,000 square feet goes to Priya Raman, the estimator, to price on site. A smaller roof gets the standard price sheet by email.
fields.tab_content_4:
212 shoppers asked when the backpack returns

When the Ridgeline 30L backpack sold out, Marlow Supply kept it on its backpacks page with a Notify me form. By restock day, 212 shoppers had left an email. When the store's API reported new stock, the app emailed all 212 and switched the card back to Add to cart.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Category Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Follow these 7 steps to plan a category landing page that leads each shopper to the right product.
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down the question a shopper brings to the category, such as "Which trail shoe fits a wide foot?" Every section of the page should help answer it. Move products that answer a different question to their own category.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Put 2 or 3 sentences above the grid that say what the category holds and who it suits. Name the attributes that set the products apart, such as cushion or drop. On a phone, the first row of products should show without a long scroll.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Label each subcategory tile with its name, such as "Pendant lights." A label like "Shop now" does not say where the link goes. Google calls good anchor text descriptive, reasonably concise, and relevant to the page it sits on and the page it links to.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Build filters from the attributes shoppers weigh, such as width or price, and keep each one as a column in the product table. Show how many products match each option. Drop a filter that leaves a shopper with fewer than 2 products.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Show price and stock on each card
fields.howto_step_5_des: Put the price and the stock status on every product card, next to one clear photo. Mark sold-out items plainly instead of hiding them. A shopper should be able to compare 2 products without opening either page.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Keep filter URLs out of the crawl
fields.howto_step_6_des: Each filter combination can create its own URL. Google's crawling guide says to use robots.txt to disallow crawling of faceted navigation URLs. Leave the main category URL and every subcategory page open to crawlers.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Reorder tiles by clicks each month
fields.howto_step_7_des: Once a month, sort the subcategory tiles by their click counts and move the busiest tile to the front. If a tile gets few clicks, try a clearer label first. Move one tile per month, so you can tell which change shifted the clicks.

faq_plan.q: What is a category landing page?
faq_plan.a: A category landing page is the page that gathers every product in one category, such as trail running shoes, under a short intro. It sits between the homepage and the product pages. Shoppers use its subcategory links and filters to narrow the range before they open a single product.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a category landing page?
faq_plan.a: Start with the product table: one row per product, with a column for each attribute shoppers compare. Then describe the page to Emergent's AI landing page builder, naming the subcategories and the filters you want. It builds the page and the table, and you change either one by prompt.

faq_plan.q: What should an ecommerce category landing page show above the product grid?
faq_plan.a: It should show a heading that names the category and a short intro, then the subcategory links and the first row of products. On an ecommerce category landing page, keep any promotion to one line: a tall banner pushes the first products below the fold.

faq_plan.q: Do category landing pages work for services as well as products?
faq_plan.a: They work for services too: a services business can group its offers the same way, with one page per category and a quote form in place of a cart. The structure works for open roles too: recruiting landing pages can group jobs by team, with a filter for location.

faq_plan.q: How many filters should a category landing page offer?
faq_plan.a: Offer as few as your range needs: start with the attributes shoppers ask about before they buy, and add a filter only when it splits the range into useful groups. If every product shares the same value, the filter does nothing and can go. On a page Emergent built, adding a filter takes one prompt naming the column.

faq_plan.q: Should every filter combination on a category landing page get its own URL?
faq_plan.a: Not unless the combination answers a search people make, such as wide trail running shoes, and deserves its own intro. Google's guide says that if your filtering mechanism is based on URL fragments, it will have no impact on crawling. That suits combinations you do not want in search.

faq_plan.q: How should filters on a category landing page work on a phone?
faq_plan.a: Put the filters behind one button above the grid, and show the number of matching products on that button as shoppers choose. A filter panel that opens over the grid keeps the products in view once it closes. The rule for any mobile landing page applies here too: every tap target should be easy to hit with a thumb.

faq_plan.q: How long should the intro on a category landing page be?
faq_plan.a: Short enough that the first row of products still shows on a phone, with longer buying advice placed below the grid. The intro tells shoppers they are in the right place. A buying guide at the bottom can explain terms such as heel drop for the shoppers who scroll that far.

faq_plan.q: How is a category landing page different from a subcategory page?
faq_plan.a: A category page covers a whole range, such as lighting, and links down to narrower pages. A subcategory page covers one slice of it, such as pendant lights, and leads straight to the products. On a site Emergent builds, both pages can read from the same product table.

faq_plan.q: Can a category landing page list things other than products?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Any set of items that people compare can sit on a category page, such as courses or rental listings. A real estate landing page can group homes by neighborhood the way a store groups shoes by width. Emergent builds the item table behind the page, and each listing is a row in a database you own.

findings.quote: Landingi / Leadpages / Instapage ... Tiered by traffic on most plans
findings.issue: The grouped column puts Leadpages under a traffic-tiered pricing claim. The library's own, newer Leadpages entry says 'No traffic caps' (https://www.leadpages.com/pricing, 'no traffic caps on any plan', checked 2026-10-12), so the column states a false fact about a named competitor. The grouped entry is the older 2026-09-28 fact; Instapage and Landingi have their own separately vetted entries. No duplicate vendor columns otherwise (Unbounce, the group, Wix each appear once).
findings.fix: Regenerate the table with separately vetted vendors instead of the group, e.g. hubctl table <url> --vs Unbounce,Leadpages,Instapage --rows build,data,visitors,abtest,ownership (Leadpages: 'No traffic caps'; Instapage: 'Monthly visitor caps by plan'), or replace the group with Landingi alone. Coordinator: the group entry in rules/competitors/lp.json contradicts the Leadpages entry and sits on about 21 LP specs.
